title: Ang 830–831: the ninth Guru in Bilaval
tomorrow: what would a week look like if every day pointed to one name?

cards: Someone's grandmother is in the hospital, and the family group chat goes quiet. Everyone loves her. Nobody can fix it.
On ang 830, Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, sings straight into that kind of silence. His answer has old stories in it, and an elephant.

teach.b: Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns in Bilaval are short, and they circle one question: in trouble, who helps? His answer, in paraphrase: know the Lord's Name as the remover of pain.
Remembering it, Ajamal and Ganika were set free. The elephant's terror ended in a moment, as soon as he called on the Lord.
These are stories from older Indian tradition: a man who had strayed, a courtesan, an elephant caught in the water. The next hymn presses harder. In paraphrase: without the Lord, no one is your help.
Whose mother, father, child or wife?
Who is anyone's brother? It sounds cold until you hear it in that quiet group chat. The Guru isn't saying family doesn't love you.
He's saying love can't always reach in, and the Name can. Now a neighbor.

teach.h: A NEIGHBOR: A VERY PRESENT HELP.
teach.b: Jews and Christians both pray the Psalms, and Psalm 46 opens, in the King James words: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble."
The same question, and the answer points the same way: help in trouble, near, from God. And one honest difference. The psalm speaks as "we," a whole people, and goes on to say they will not fear.
The ninth Guru speaks to one mind at a time, and points it to the Name, remembered. Two traditions side by side, neither one needing the other to be wrong.

how: Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns are sung in kirtan like the other Gurus'; his Bilaval hymns on ang 830–831 name Ajamal, Ganika and the elephant as those freed by remembering the Name.

s: the ninth Guru says your family doesn't love you
he says love can't always reach in; the Name can.
Guru Tegh Bahadur names Ajamal, Ganika and an elephant in Bilaval
each was freed by remembering the Lord's Name.
Psalm 46 and the ninth Guru's hymn say exactly the same thing
both point to God's help in trouble; the psalm speaks as 'we,' the Guru to one mind and the Name.

games.q: a classmate who isn't religious asks: 'if your family loves you, why would you need God in a crisis?' by the ninth Guru's hymn, what's the best answer?
o: love is real, but it can't always reach in; the Guru points to a help that can.
family love doesn't really count; only God's love does.
you don't need anything; a crisis passes on its own.
games.why: the hymn asks 'who is anyone's brother?' not to dismiss family, but to say where help reaches when love can't.

practice: Count slowly on your fingers the times help came when you couldn't help yourself: a person, a call, a door that opened. Stop at whatever number feels true, and rest with your hand open for the rest of the sit.
If you'd like, read the hymns on ang 830 first.
